source.title: fmxcoders: Factorized Masked Crosscoders for Cross-Layer Feature Discovery
source.authors: A. Demou; Panagiotis Koromilas; James Oldfield; Yannis Panagakis; M. Nicolaou

record.tranche_reason: The study measures cross-layer latent coherence and semantic-versus-surface categories using methods different from the original vision-neuron examples. It tests architecture/regularization and measurement-related versions, but does not directly test whether ordinary individual language-model neurons respond to unrelated inputs.
record.gate_note: The study reports results on crosscoder and fmxcoder latents, not on individual neurons’ responses to unrelated input categories in the sense of the claim’s canonical examples. Its central outcome measures—functional coherence and LLM-judged semantic/surface counts—bear on V5 and V7. Results cited from prior work are not recorded as rows. Reconstruction and probing metrics are included only where they assess the performance trade-off relevant to V5.
record.test_reason: The study trains cross-layer sparse dictionaries (crosscoders and its own fmxcoders) on LLM residual-stream activations. It reports how many layers drive each latent, judge-labelled semantic versus surface latent counts, and reconstruction and probing scores of its own method against baselines. It never measures whether the base models' MLP neurons, or any model units, respond to unrelated inputs. Dictionary learning rests on the superposition/polysemanticity premise, but here it is only a tool. Functional coherence measures layer dependence, not polysemanticity. Semantic versus surface counts describe the dictionary's latents, not the network's neurons. Toggling the dictionary's parameterization does not change the share of polysemantic neurons in the language model. So the reader's V5 and V7 links do not hold.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that standard crosscoders mostly learn layer-localized, surface-pattern latents despite evenly spread decoder norms. Tensor factorization combined with stochastic layer masking roughly doubles functional coherence and yields about an order of magnitude more semantic latents. Reconstruction (MSE down 25–50%) and probing F1 (up 10–30 points) also improve. Masking costs 4–9 F1 points relative to the unmasked fmxcoder.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains factorized cross-layer dictionaries with stochastic layer masking and evaluates coherence, semantic/surface counts, reconstruction, and sparse probes. It does not reproduce the original neuron-level vision analysis or the Softmax Linear Units method.
record.method_sensitivity: Functional coherence rises with masking probability in the Pythia-410M ablations; factorization alone does not increase it. Norm coherence and functional coherence give substantially different impressions of layer dependence. The paper also notes model- and dataset-dependent settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Standard crosscoder latents have high decoder-norm coherence (about 7.7) but low functional coherence (about 2), so each latent is driven by one or two layers. Factorization plus layer masking roughly doubles functional coherence (3.8 on Pythia-410M).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Crosscoder latents that look cross-layer by decoder norms are functionally layer-localized.

fits_no_version.finding: fmxcoders yield 3–13× more GPT-4o-mini-judged semantic latents than crosscoders across four LLMs. Low-coherence latents are surface patterns such as digits and punctuation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-layer dictionary latents with higher functional coherence are more often semantic concept detectors.

record.problems: The experiments use only eight middle post-MLP residual-stream locations, one sparsifier and fixed dictionary width. The judge-based semantic/surface distinction may be unreliable, and the main results use a single training run per LLM/fmxcoder variant. The study evaluates cross-layer dictionary latents rather than the claimed individual-neuron behavior.
record.rows_left_out: Reconstruction EV and cosine similarity, Wasserstein distances, detailed per-dataset probe scores, and CP-fmxcoder tables were not extracted as separate rows; they are secondary performance measures and do not directly measure the coherence or semantic-category outcomes recorded here. See Tables 3–5 and Appendix B.

untested.parts: No measurement of how many LLM MLP neurons respond to unrelated tokens.
Superposition is not tested as a cause of neuron polysemanticity.
Initialization, regularization or noise are not tested as sources of neuron polysemanticity.
The base models' architecture or training is not varied, and the share of polysemantic neurons is not measured. Only the dictionary parameterization changes.
Canonical polysemantic neurons are not re-examined.
No neuron polysemanticity measurement is compared across activation ranges or scoring methods. The norm vs functional coherence comparison concerns layer spread.

record.verdict_notes: The reader mapped dictionary-latent properties onto neuron polysemanticity. This study is about cross-layer dictionary learning. It assumes the dictionary-learning framework but makes no measurement of polysemantic neurons, so no verdicts are given and the reader's V5/V7 labels are removed.

versions.untested_parts: Vision classifiers, InceptionV1, and neuron 4e:55 are not studied.
The study does not measure how often individual MLP neurons in language models respond to unrelated tokens or contexts. Its subjects are cross-layer dictionary latents.
The study does not test whether polysemanticity is caused by representing more sparse features than there are neurons or by packing features through superposition.
Initialization and training noise as causes of polysemanticity without capacity pressure are not tested.

The study compares crosscoder parameterizations and layer masking, not activation functions or modern convolutional networks. It studies cross-layer latents rather than the share of ordinary model neurons that are polysemantic.
The study does not re-examine canonical polysemantic neurons or show that apparently unrelated inputs share a feature such as pose.
The study compares norm-based and functional coherence, but does not systematically vary activation-range cutoffs or compare alternative explanation-scoring methods.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: fmxcoder versus standard crosscoder on the four tested base LLMs
reader_labels.reason: Masked fmxcoders have more judge-labeled semantic latents in all four models (r11–r14); the Pythia-410M masked model also has higher functional coherence than the unmasked or standard crosscoder measures (r5–r8).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: p=0.05 masked fmxcoders on the four tested base LLMs
reader_labels.reason: The masked variants have lower probing F1 than the unmasked fmxcoders, although their F1 remains above the standard crosscoder values; this is a feature-probing trade-off, not a general model-capability test (r23–r30).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Pythia-410M crosscoder and fmxcoder coherence measures
reader_labels.reason: Norm coherence stays high (about 7) while functional coherence is about 2 for standard crosscoders and rises for the masked fmxcoder, showing that conclusions about layer distribution depend on which measure is used (r1–r8).
